source_topic: Control premium implied by an EV multiple

follow_up.question: Why can an EV premium differ from an equity premium?
follow_up.reference: Net debt changes the base against which enterprise value and equity value are measured. The same dollar uplift is a different proportion of each base.

instances.text: Consider a retailer. Apply 14.5 times to EBITDA of 180 million dollars. Net debt is 125 million dollars; there are 40 million shares. The unaffected price is 35 dollars. What control premium does the implied offer represent, as a percentage?

What control premium does the implied offer represent, as a percentage?

follow_up.question: What if the target held net cash instead of net debt?
follow_up.reference: Net cash would increase the equity value implied by a fixed enterprise value. Apply its sign consistently when bridging to the offer price.

instances.spoken_text: Consider a distributor. Apply fifteen times to EBITDA of one hundred and ninety million dollars. Net debt is two hundred and seventy-five million dollars; there are sixty million shares. The unaffected price is thirty-five dollars. What control premium does the implied offer represent, as a percentage?

follow_up.question: Why use the unaffected share count and price together?
follow_up.reference: Their product gives the unaffected market value of the same common equity claims. Mixing diluted and basic share counts could create a false premium.

follow_up.reference: It inherits whatever economics are embedded in the precedent multiple. A separate synergy estimate is needed to judge whether that price is justified.

follow_up.reference: Net debt changes the base against which enterprise value and equity value are measured. The same dollar uplift is a different proportion of each base.
